title: HE CUT OFF THE THUMBS AND BIG TOES OF SEVENTY KINGS—THEN GOD ALLOWED THE SAME THING TO HAPPEN TO HIM
paragraphs: HE CUT OFF THE THUMBS AND BIG TOES OF SEVENTY KINGS—THEN GOD ALLOWED THE SAME THING TO HAPPEN TO HIM

He thought the suffering of other men was proof of his greatness. Then one terrible day, the cruelty he had inflicted on seventy kings came back to him. But buried inside this disturbing Bible story is a warning about sin, a revelation about God's justice, and a Gospel truth that could change the way you see your own past forever.
“As I have done, so God hath requited me.” — Judges 1:7 (KJV)
Imagine being a king.
Not an ordinary king.
A king so feared that other kings trembled at the mention of your name.
You have conquered cities. Humiliated rulers. Broken men who once commanded armies.
And beneath your table...
Seventy defeated kings are gathering scraps of food.
Not servants.
Not prisoners awaiting trial.
Kings.
Men who once sat on thrones, wore crowns, issued commands, and believed their kingdoms would never fall.
But now they cannot even pick up their food the way they once did.
Because you had their thumbs cut off.
And their big toes.
Seventy kings.
Seventy lives deliberately humiliated.
And somehow, you convinced yourself that their suffering was a monument to your power.
Until the day another army came.
Until the day you became the prisoner.
Until the day someone reached for your hands.
And suddenly...
You understood.
The man who had spent years making other kings helpless was about to discover what helplessness felt like.
And what he said afterward is one of the most chilling confessions in the Old Testament.
But before you distance yourself from this ancient king, before you decide that this story has nothing to do with your life, consider something.
You do not need a crown to become cruel.
You do not need a throne to worship power.
And you do not need to cut off someone's fingers to leave wounds that follow them for years.
Sometimes the most dangerous throne is the one we build inside our hearts.
And sometimes the person sitting on it is us.
The Bible introduces this king in Judges 1:4–7.
His name was Adoni-bezek.
The name אֲדֹנִי־בֶזֶק (ʾAdonî-Bezeq) is commonly understood to mean “lord of Bezek,” identifying him by his authority or association with Bezek.
The setting is important.
Joshua had died, and the book of Judges opens with Israel seeking the LORD's direction concerning the battles ahead. Judah was instructed to go first, and Simeon joined Judah in the campaign.
Judges 1:4–5 records that Judah went up, the LORD delivered the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hand, and they encountered Adoni-bezek at Bezek.
Then came the terrible reversal.
The King James Version records:

“And they found Adonibezek in Bezek: and they fought against him, and they slew the Canaanites and the Perizzites. But Adonibezek fled; and they pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes.” — Judges 1:5–6
Pause there.
He fled.
The man who had made others run for their lives was now running for his own.
He was caught.
The man who had held others captive was now in captivity.
And the same mutilation he had imposed upon defeated kings was inflicted upon him.
Scripture does not invite us to enjoy this violence. It records a brutal event in Israel's ancient history and then allows the defeated king's own words to expose the significance he saw in it.
Listen carefully to his confession.

“And Adonibezek said, Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me. And they brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died.” — Judges 1:7 (KJV)
“As I have done, so God hath requited me.”
There is an entire sermon inside that sentence.
And perhaps an entire lifetime of regret.
In the Hebrew text, the confession ends:
כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתִי כֵּן שִׁלַּם־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Ka'asher asiti, ken shillam-li Elohim.
A close translation is:
“As I have done, so God has repaid me.”
The Hebrew verb שִׁלַּם (shillam) comes from a verb that can express paying, repaying, or making recompense.
The king himself interpreted what happened to him as divine repayment.
Notice that distinction.
The text records his confession. It does not provide us with permission to declare that every person who suffers is being punished for something they have done.
Jesus explicitly challenged that kind of simplistic judgment in Luke 13:1–5 and John 9:1–3.
But in this particular account, Adoni-bezek recognized a devastating correspondence between his own cruelty and what had happened to him.
He had stripped others of their dignity.
Now his dignity was stripped away.
He had treated kings like animals beneath his table.
Now he was no longer sitting above anyone.
And the throne that once made him feel untouchable could not save him.
Can you imagine the silence that followed his confession?
No boasting.
No royal decree.
No army rushing to rescue him.
Just a defeated man confronting the reality of what he had done.
The text does not tell us everything he thought or felt. We cannot know whether his words expressed genuine repentance or simply an acknowledgment that judgment had caught up with him.
But we know what he said.
“As I have done...”
Four words that reveal a terrible moment of recognition.
And there is something deeply unsettling about those words.
Because sometimes the consequences of our actions do not arrive immediately.
Sometimes pride is rewarded for a season.
Sometimes cruelty looks like strength.
Sometimes deception produces temporary success.
Sometimes a person can hurt others, move on, build a comfortable life, and convince themselves that nothing will ever come of it.
But a delayed consequence is not proof that God is indifferent.
Ecclesiastes 8:11 warns that when judgment against evil is not carried out speedily, the human heart can become emboldened to do wrong.
That is a frightening possibility.
Not because God is impatient.
But because human beings can mistake His patience for permission.
Think about that person you humiliated when you had the advantage.
That family member whose weakness you used against them.
That friend whose trust you betrayed.
That employee you treated as though their dignity depended on your approval.
That spouse who kept asking to be heard while you kept insisting on being right.
Or perhaps you were the one sitting beneath someone else's table.
The one who was mocked.
The one who was manipulated.
The one whose pain became somebody else's entertainment.
The one who learned to remain silent because speaking only made things worse.
This story speaks to both sides of that suffering.
To the person who has abused power, it says that power does not erase accountability.
To the person who has been wounded by someone powerful, it says that the person who harmed you is not beyond God's sight.
But there is something else we must understand.
God's justice is real. Yet God's justice is not an invitation for us to become cruel in return.
That distinction matters.
The book of Judges describes many violent and morally disturbing events. Not everything recorded in its pages is presented as an example for Christians to imitate.
The mutilation of Adoni-bezek is part of the narrative, not a command for believers to punish their enemies in the same way.
Jesus calls His followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:44).
Paul writes:
That does not mean injustice should be ignored.
It does not mean victims must remain in dangerous situations.
It does not mean abusers should escape accountability.
Seeking protection, establishing boundaries, telling the truth, and pursuing lawful justice can all be consistent with Christian faithfulness.
It means that revenge must not become the god of our hearts.
Because when we allow another person's cruelty to transform us into someone equally cruel, their sin has begun shaping our character.
And Jesus calls us to something greater.
But now comes the question that changes the direction of this entire story.
What happens when you are not simply the person who has been hurt?
What happens when you realize you have also hurt others?
What happens when you cannot honestly say you were always the victim?
What happens when you remember the lies you told, the people you used, the promises you broke, and the opportunities you had to do right but deliberately chose wrong?
What happens when your conscience begins whispering...
“As I have done...”
Perhaps you have never been a king.
But you know what it means to regret something.
You know what it means to replay a conversation in your mind and wish you could take your words back.
You know what it means to look at an old photograph and remember a version of yourself you are ashamed of.
You know what it means to lie awake wondering whether you have gone too far.
And perhaps the hardest part is this:
You cannot go backward.
You cannot unsay the words.
You cannot recover every opportunity.
You cannot erase every consequence.
You cannot make every wounded person trust you again.
So what do you do when the past is real, the damage is real, and your guilt is real?
This is where the story of a defeated king leads us to something far greater than the story itself.
It leads us to the Gospel.
Not because Judges 1:4–7 secretly describes the crucifixion. It does not.
Not because Adoni-bezek is presented as a direct prophecy of Jesus. He is not.
But because this account raises a question the Gospel answers with breathtaking clarity.
How can guilty people stand before a holy and just God?
Adoni-bezek could recognize that he had received a consequence resembling the cruelty he had inflicted.
But recognition alone is not the same as redemption.
A person can admit wrongdoing and still remain unchanged.
A person can fear consequences without loving righteousness.
A person can regret being caught without grieving the evil they committed.
True repentance goes deeper.
It means turning toward God, acknowledging sin without excuses, and seeking the transformation that only His grace can accomplish.
And here is the glorious difference between merely facing the consequences of sin and receiving salvation in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not say that sin is harmless. It says that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
Not just ancient tyrants.
Not just violent rulers.
Not just people whose failures became public scandals.
All of us.
The respectable person.
The religious person.
The person who looks faithful on Sunday but secretly struggles through the week.
The person who knows the right Bible verses but has not surrendered the hidden parts of their life.
The person who has been harmed.
And the person who has done harm.
All of us need grace.
And the wonder of Christianity is not that God pretends our sins never happened.
It is that God has acted in history through His Son to reconcile sinners to Himself.
At the cross, Jesus did not excuse evil.
He bore sin.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
Centuries later, the apostle Peter applied the suffering of Christ to our salvation.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God...” — 1 Peter 3:18 (KJV)
Read that again.
The just for the unjust.
The innocent for the guilty.
The righteous One suffering to bring sinners to God.
Adoni-bezek's story shows a man who recognized the return of his own cruelty.
The cross shows us the sinless Savior who willingly suffered for sins He never committed.
That is not a small distinction.
That is the heart of redemption.
Jesus Christ was not another fallen king being punished for His own wrongdoing.
He was the holy Son of God who gave Himself for sinners.
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin and death would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is why the Gospel is more than a message about becoming a better person.
It is the announcement of what God has done through Jesus Christ.
It is the call to repent and believe.
It is the promise that forgiveness is available through Him.
It is the beginning of a transformed life.
The Greek word often translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It refers to a change of mind or understanding and, in biblical calls to repentance, carries the demand to turn away from sin toward God.
When Jesus proclaimed, “Repent ye, and believe the gospel” in Mark 1:15, He was not merely inviting people to feel sorry.
He was calling them to respond to the arrival of God's kingdom.
To turn.
To believe.
To surrender.
To follow.
And perhaps that is the word someone reading this needs today.
Turn.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more secret compromise.
Not after you have convinced everyone you are fine.
Turn to Jesus Christ.
You do not have to invent a better past before coming to Him.
You cannot.
But you can come honestly.
You can confess what you have done.
You can stop defending what God calls sin.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can begin making restitution where appropriate and possible.
You can ask the Holy Spirit to transform the habits that have harmed you and others.
And you can trust that the grace of Christ is greater than the power of sin to define your eternal destiny.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
A forgiven person may still need to rebuild trust.
A repentant person may still need to face legal consequences.
A restored believer may still carry painful memories.
Grace is not a way to escape responsibility.
Grace is the gift that makes a new life possible without denying the truth about the old one.
Consider the apostle Paul.
Before he became one of the most influential witnesses to Jesus Christ, he persecuted the church.
He approved of Stephen's death and sought to imprison believers.
He later described himself as a former blasphemer, persecutor, and injurious man.
Yet he wrote:
“And the grace of our Lord was exceeding abundant with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.” — 1 Timothy 1:14 (KJV)
Paul never needed to pretend that his past was innocent.
He testified that Christ had shown him mercy.
And that mercy changed the direction of his life.
The persecutor became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The man who once sought to silence Christians became a witness willing to suffer for Christ.
That is transformation.
Not a rewritten historical record.
A redeemed life.
And that is what we mean when we say:
Jesus does not rewrite history by making yesterday's evil good.
He rewrites the story of a redeemed life by giving the forgiven sinner a new identity, a new direction, and an eternal hope.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It may explain some of your fears.
It may explain why certain memories still bring tears to your eyes.
But through Jesus Christ, your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
Notice the words.
In Christ.
Not simply religious.
Not merely inspired.
Not just emotionally moved by a powerful story.
In Christ.
United to Him by faith.
Forgiven through His sacrifice.
Made new by His grace.
This is why I do not want you to finish this article merely thinking about a king who lost his thumbs and big toes.
I want you to think about the King who bore the wounds of crucifixion.
The King who did not use His authority to exploit the helpless.
The King who washed His disciples' feet.
The King who welcomed repentant sinners.
The King who spoke forgiveness even while suffering.
The King who conquered death.
The King whose throne will never collapse.
Jesus Christ.
Adoni-bezek used power to bring other kings beneath his table.
Jesus used His authority to serve, and through His death and resurrection He opens the way for sinners to come to God.
One king made weakness an object of humiliation.
The true King of kings displayed His love through sacrificial suffering.
One king's confession was, “As I have done, so God hath requited me.”
But the song of the redeemed is different.
Not because we deserve better.
But because Christ has shown mercy.
And if that truth is beginning to break through the walls you have built around your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe you have been living with hidden guilt.
Maybe you have been asking God why your life feels so empty despite everything you have achieved.
Maybe you have been carrying anger toward someone who treated you as though you were worthless.
Maybe you have been trying to punish yourself for sins Jesus calls you to confess and forsake.
Or maybe you have been using your own pain as permission to wound other people.
Whatever brought you here, the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
Not with a performance.
Not with a polished explanation.
Not with a list of reasons why your sin was understandable.
Come in truth.
Come in repentance.
Come in faith.
And receive the mercy He freely offers.
If you need words to express that surrender, you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have tried to justify things I should have confessed. I have carried guilt, pride, bitterness, and wounds that I cannot heal by myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to repent sincerely, to make right what I can, to forgive as You command, and to walk in obedience to Your Word. I surrender my life to You. Change my heart and make me more like You. In Your name, amen.”
A prayer is not a magical formula. Our hope rests in Jesus Christ Himself, not in the mere repetition of words.
And if you have prayed sincerely, do not treat this as the end of your journey.
Open your Bible.
Seek a faithful local church.
Grow in prayer.
Learn to obey Christ.
Walk with believers who will encourage you, correct you when necessary, and remind you of the Gospel when your strength feels small.
Because following Jesus is not about experiencing one emotional moment and returning unchanged to the life you were living.
It is about belonging to Him.
Day after day.
Even when nobody is watching.
Even when obedience is costly.
Even when the old habits call your name.
Even when healing takes longer than you expected.
And perhaps this is where your own story can become an encouragement to someone else.
And please, do not let this message stop with you.
Not because a social media post makes anyone more righteous.
But because someone among your family, friends, or followers may be carrying a burden they have never told anyone about.
Someone may be living with regret.
Someone may have stopped believing that forgiveness is possible.
Someone may be standing at the edge of giving up on faith.
Your simple act of sharing could place the truth of Scripture before someone who desperately needs to hear it.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe this ministry is worth helping to sustain.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep pointing people toward the Lord Jesus Christ through biblical content, Gospel-centered storytelling, Christian books, devotionals, and discipleship resources.
Behind every article is a continuing mission to reach people, encourage believers, and make resources available to those who want to grow deeper in their understanding of Scripture.
We want that work to continue.
And, by God's grace, we want it to reach even more people.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Those words matter to us.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.
These are small, tangible ways we want to express our appreciation to those who help this ministry continue.
The greater purpose, however, is not merchandise.
It is helping people open their Bibles again.
It is encouraging believers to stand firm when life becomes difficult.
It is reaching the person who feels too ashamed to enter a church.
It is pointing the wounded toward Christ, the proud toward repentance, the weary toward His promises, and the lost toward the Savior.
If that is a mission you believe is worth supporting, I warmly invite you to become part of it.
The Gospel must never be placed behind a price tag.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
His grace cannot be purchased.
And your value before God is not measured by a monthly contribution.
What matters eternally is whether you belong to Christ.
That brings us back to the king at Bezek.
The king who once believed he could do anything he wanted.
The king who made seventy other kings gather scraps beneath his table.
The king who fled when his own power collapsed.
The king whose final recorded words confronted the cruelty of his past.
“As I have done, so God hath requited me.”
His story ends with his death in Jerusalem.
There is no recorded restoration.
No recorded conversion.
No recorded second chance.
Scripture does not tell us his eternal destiny, and we should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But Scripture has revealed something wonderful about Jesus Christ.
He receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
He calls the proud to humble themselves.
He calls the guilty to repent.
He calls the wounded to trust His justice rather than surrender their hearts to revenge.
He calls His people to live differently because His grace has changed them.
And He promises:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
That promise is worth remembering when shame tells you not to pray.
When regret tells you that you are beyond forgiveness.
When pride tells you that you do not need forgiveness.
When fear tells you that your past is stronger than the cross.
The king at Bezek could not return to the moment before he committed his cruelties.
Neither can you return to yesterday.
But today, while you still have breath, you can turn to the living Christ.
You can tell the truth.
You can repent.
You can believe.
You can begin walking in the newness of life that His grace makes possible.
And years from now, when someone asks what happened to the person you used to be, may your answer not be a story about how you made yourself righteous.
May it be a testimony about the Savior who showed you mercy.
Because the most devastating thing about your past is not that you cannot change what happened—it is the tragedy of refusing the Savior who can change what happens next.
